text: The Mike Wallace interview presented by the American Broadcasting Company in association
with the Fund for the Republic brings you a special television series discussing the
problems of survival and freedom in America.
Good evening, I'm Mike Wallace.
In recent weeks, we've been discussing the problems of a free society and what it must
do to survive.
It will try to measure the impact of our free society on us as individuals, whether we're
as happy as we like to think we are or as free to think and to feel.
Our guest is Dr. Eric Fromm, a psychoanalyst and social critic who is internationally renowned
for his studies of men and their search for freedom.
Dr. Fromm, first let me ask you this, from many different quarters, the United States,
who I think you will agree has been criticized as a materialistic society, perhaps even a
shallow society.
Yet only recently you said this.
You said there has never been a better society than in the United States in 1958.
What do you mean by that?
Well, I mean it, of course, in relative terms.
The history of man so far is nothing to brag about from the standpoint of our ideals.
But what I mean is that in comparison with most other societies, our presently American
society has achieved things which are remarkable, material wealth greater than for any other
nation, relative freedom from oppression, relative mobility, spreading of art, of music, of thought,
which is also rather unique.
So I would say compared with the 19th century, compared with most previous history, this
is as good a better society.
shallow. We are actually afraid to be intimate with people, many people even
with their wives and husbands. And we substitute or we rather hide this fear of
real intimacy by a superficial kind of friendliness which is quite nice but
nevertheless very shallow. But I think there is another answer to your question
which I should like to give. Actually, if you take the average American and
studies have shown that. He is really concerned only with private affairs. That
is to say with his health, his money and family affairs. He is not concerned with
his society. He talks about it. But you know if one speaks of being concerned I
mean something about which one loses one's sleep sometime. And the average American
never loses his sleep about affairs which relate to his society and to
our whole country. That is to say I mean he has separated his private life from
his existence as a member of his society and leaves that to the specialist in the
government to take care. Do you think that that is happening to American men?
And of course we're speaking not only of American men but American women as well
here Dr. Fromme. In relationship to his politics, to his political beliefs? Yes
indeed. We have in the same way relegated our own responsibility in what happens
to our country to the specialist who are supposed to take care of it and
individual citizen does not feel that he can judge and even that he should judge
and take any responsibility. I think there are quite a number of recent
developments which show that. Like for instance? Like for instance that we are
confronted with a possibility of a war of such destruction that the whole
existence of our nation and of the whole world is at stake. And yet people know
it. People read it in the newspaper. People read that if the first attack a
hundred million Americans might be killed. And yet they talk about it as
if they were talking about something being wrong with a carburetor of their
car perhaps. Actually they have paid more attention to the danger of a flu
